newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NOT MUCH UPSIDE IN BEING LONG OLOS VS BUNDS - JPM.
newsitem.headline: NOT MUCH UPSIDE IN BEING LONG OLOS VS BUNDS - JPM.

text.p: The tight spread of Belgian government bonds over Bunds, disadvantageous funding and the remote risk of an EMU delay meant there was not much upside in being long OLOs against Bunds now, JP Morgan said in a report.

It expected the 10-year spread over Bunds to rise marginally to over 10 basis points in the coming weeks, noting in its Market Views that the yield differential was stuck in a tight range and that independent yield curve moves were non-existent.
The spread was unchanged at seven basis points at 1025 GMT on Tuesday in a becalmed market which saw early pressure from weaker Treasuries on Bunds fade.

Dealers expected the market to remain range-bound, eyeing key levels on the Bund future at 100.90 and 101.43. The German September contract was down 0.02 at 101.27 at 1035 GMT, its Belgian equivalent up 0.11 at 120.85.
The Belgian future benefitted somewhat from rollover business out of June which expires on Wednesday.

Dealers said the market might eke some direction out of U.S. May consumer confidence data due at 1400 GMT and forecast to show weakness, but with expectations in general for unchanged U.S. interest rates in the short term such data would only provide confirmation and no new trend.

Since the July 1-2 U.S. FOMC meeting is widely forecast to hold rates steady, any fireworks would have to come from the June jobs report, also due next week. OLOs and futures needed signs of stronger growth and inflation to pry prices loose from current levels, dealers said. Evidence of strength was more likely to come from the buoyant U.S. than from sluggish Europe.

On the domestic front the National Bank economic indicator and CPI would also not stir prices, analysts said. CPI might rise due to seasonally higher vegetable and fresh fruit prices and dollar-driven import prices to 0.1 month-on-month and 1.7 percent year-on-year, but the overall picture was still benign.

There was no noticeable impact from comments by Belgian Budget Minister Herman Van Rompuy, who in a newspaper interview confirmed Belgium's commitment to curbing its budget deficit and to its entry into EMU from the planned 1999 start.
He said the deficit as a percentage of GDP would be "just below 2.9 percent this year, with a little bit of luck." In 1996 the ratio was 3.2 percent, he said, quoting National Bank figures.
Among the criteria for entry into Europe's single currency union, the Maastricht Treaty stipulates that a country's budget deficit must amount to no more than three percent.
